section: Calculate the proportion of Netflix’s catlog that is globally available.
text:
Calculate the proportion of Netflix’s catlog that is globally available.

global_fraction_stats <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(
    title_fraction = n_distinct(title[available_globally %in% TRUE]) /
      n_distinct(title),
    hours_fraction = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally %in% TRUE]) /
      sum(hours_viewed)
  )
global_fraction_stats |>
  mutate(
    title_fraction = scales::percent(title_fraction, accuracy = 0.1),
    hours_fraction = scales::percent(hours_fraction, accuracy = 0.1)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  title_fraction hours_fraction
  <chr>          <chr>         
1 24.6%          51.9%         


This dataset covers statistical results from 2023 to the first half of 2026, featuring a total of 24,427 movies and shows. Both “Bridgerton universe” and “Beyond Stranger Things” generated nearly 5 billion hours of view time, making them considered as “popular Netflix series”. In the first half of 2026, the top 10 most-watched titles accounted for 6.70% of total view time. Only 24.6% of Netflix’s content library is available worldwide, representing just 5.19% of total runtime. ## top title(by total hours viewed) in each period & fraction of total viewership

top_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(period_total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  slice_max(order_by = hours_viewed, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(viewership_share = hours_viewed / period_total) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, viewership_share) 
  
  top_titles |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(columns = viewership_share) |>
  fmt_number(columns = hours_viewed, decimals = 0, use_seps = TRUE)

section: Across each period, audiences spent varying proportions of their time watching episodic shows compared to feature films.
text:
Across each period, audiences spent varying proportions of their time watching episodic shows compared to feature films.

tv_movie_stats <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      runtime > 240 | str_detect(title, "Season"),
      "Show",
      "Movie"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarize(
    hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop_last"
  ) |>
  mutate(time_fraction = hours_viewed / sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, content_type, time_fraction) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = content_type,
    values_from = time_fraction
  )

  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(Movie, Show))

section: What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available? (Answer this both by title and weighted by hours viewed)
text:
What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available? (Answer this both by title and weighted by hours viewed)


Code
global_fraction_stats <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(
    title_fraction = n_distinct(title[available_globally %in% TRUE]) /
      n_distinct(title),
    hours_fraction = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally %in% TRUE], na.rm = TRUE) /
      sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  )


By title, 24.6% of Netflix’s catalog is globally available, while weighted by hours viewed, that fraction is 51.9%.

text:

  slice_max(order_by = hours_viewed, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(viewership_share = hours_viewed / period_total) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, viewership_share)

    tab_header(

      columns = viewership_share,
      decimals = 2

section: How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? (You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.)
text:
How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? (You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.)


Code
catalog_stats <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(
    number_titles = n_distinct(title),
    total_runtime_minutes = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) 
catalog_stats |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Catalog Size Over Time"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(number_titles, total_runtime_minutes),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  )

This table shows that from 2023H1 to 2023H2, although the number_titles dropped from 18,126 to 6,574, the total_runtime_minutes increased from 2,623,021 to 3,007,003. Furthermore, the 2026H1 data shows that the number_titles increased to 8,163, and the total_runtime_minutes went straight up to 3,771,293. This indicates that Netflix should know what titles the audience really likes, may remove some old and unpopular titles, and add new and appealing titles after the adjustment to boost the total_runtime_minutes.

title: Data Acquisition
section: Which titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? (These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back on as ‘comfort food’, e.g., re-runs of Friends.)
text:
Which titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? (These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back on as ‘comfort food’, e.g., re-runs of Friends.)


Code
consistent_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarize(
    periods_present = n_distinct(period),
    average_hours_viewed = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_hours_viewed = min(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_hours_viewed = sd(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(periods_present == n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)) |>
  arrange(desc(min_hours_viewed)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

consistent_titles |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Top 10 Titles with Consistently High Viewership"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    title = "Title",
    periods_present = "Periods",
    average_hours_viewed = "Average Hours Viewed",
    min_hours_viewed = "Minimum Hours Viewed",
    sd_hours_viewed = "Standard Deviation"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      average_hours_viewed,
      min_hours_viewed,
      sd_hours_viewed
    ),
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  )

We could say Money Heist: Part 1 is the most consistent title because of the standard deviation 9.63M is the lowest one in the table. But the most consistently high title is Pablo Escobar: Season 1 because its has high average hours viewed of 136.21M as well as relatively low standard deviation of 22.86M.

title: Data Acquisition
section: Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?
text:
Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?


Code
tv_movie_stats <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      runtime > 240 | str_detect(title, "Season"),
      "Show",
      "Movie"
    ),
    content_type = replace_na(content_type, "Unclassified")
  ) |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarize(
    hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop_last"
  ) |>
  mutate(time_fraction = hours_viewed / sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, content_type, time_fraction) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = content_type,
    values_from = time_fraction
  )

tv_movie_stats |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "TV Shows vs. Movies: Viewing Hours by Period"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    Movie = "Movies",
    Show = "TV Shows",
    Unclassified = "Unclassified"
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(Movie, Show, Unclassified),
    decimals = 2
  )
